key_insight: A2M shows that MCP agents can be hijacked by optimizing tool metadata to attract selection and then using execution traces to manipulate outcomes through attacker-controlled tool returns.
engineering_relevance: For MCP-based agent systems, this highlights the need for stricter tool vetting, provenance checks, and runtime isolation before third-party tools are allowed to influence decisions or actions.
method: Attraction: black-box optimize tool metadata to maximize the chance an agent selects the malicious tool.
Manipulation: use execution traces to refine adversarial outputs that steer the agent toward attacker goals.
Evaluate transferability by testing attacks on other models without re-optimization.
evidence_signal: On LiveMCPBench, the attack achieved 93.6% malicious tool invocation, 32.4× token-cost inflation under Cognitive Denial of Service, and 74.4% mean attack success across three harmful scenarios; transfer to four other models still reached 63.6%, 2.7× cost, and 24.5% success.
watch_item: Results depend on black-box optimization against specific MCP behaviors, so real-world effectiveness may vary with stronger tool validation, monitoring, and tighter output sanitization.
paper_title: A2M: Trace-Optimized Agent Hijacking in the MCP Ecosystem
